newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Bankers Trust seen threat to Dutch PTT bid for TNT.
newsitem.headline: Bankers Trust seen threat to Dutch PTT bid for TNT.

text.p: The friendly A$2 billion (US$1.6 billion) bid for Australian transport group TNT Ltd by Dutch telecoms and postal group Koninklijke PTT (KPN) was thrown into doubt on Wednesday after Bankers Trust Australia revealed it had built a strategic stake in the Sydney-based company.

The local arm of the New York-based investment bank said it held 19.99 percent of TNT and would not commit itself to accepting the cash offer by the KPN which had earlier been regarded by analysts as virtually assured of success.

BT Australia said in a statement prepared for Reuters that the offer price was low and the two companies were not a good fit. "The A$2.45 bid by KPN for TNT is at a price that is at the lower end of a range of valuations we have on the company," BT Australia equities chief Rohan Hedley said.
BT's statement surprised traders and helped push TNT to near the top of the turnover list on the Australian Stock Exchange as speculation grew that BT might seek another buyer for its stake.
Federal Express Corp, the U.S.-based air freight giant, was tipped by some as a possible rival bidder to KPN.

"They (KPN) don't have a big express freight business so what they are doing is buying an express freight business whereas Federal Express have a very big express freight business virtually everywhere in the world except Europe," said one transport analyst with a European-based broker.
"So there is potential for synergies there. But at A$2.45 I think it is at the top end of the valuation," the analyst said.
BT Australia's Hedley queried KPN's forecast that the bid would raise KPN's profits.

"KPN have indicated that they expect the acquisition to be earnings-per-share positive in year one and materially so in year two, despite the fact that there are relatively few obvious synergies between the majority of businesses within the two groups," Hedley said.

Documents filed with the Australian Stock Exchange show that BT Australia now owned 117.01 million TNT shares after spending about A$43 million on the purchase of 18.04 million shares, or three percent, since the bid was announced last Wednesday.
It paid between A$2.38 and A$2.43 per share.
TNT shares closed two cents higher on Wednesday at A$2.41.
Trade was fairly light in the morning session but jumped to more than 10.35 million as news of the BT statement filtered through to the market.
Peter Struk, a dealer at Sydney broker Reynolds and Co, said institutions were seen to be active buyers of TNT stock on the basis that BT Australia could hold out for a higher price.
"The bottom line is we are just waiting to see what happens, that is really what we are doing," a BT spokeswoman said when asked if BT would accept the KPN offer.
A spokeswoman for KPN's corporate advisers said the Dutch company was aware of the substantial shareholder notice filed by with the stock exchange.
"Yes, KPN is obviously aware of this," she said. "It is the action of a single shareholder. KPN is not prepared to make any comment on it," she said.
KPN chairman Wim Dik, announcing the bid last Wednesday at a news conference alongside TNT executives, said he regarded the A$2.45 per share offer as "full and fair".
On the same day, KPN acquired a 9.9 percent stake at the offer price which was filled in about 10 minutes, one fund manager said.
The offer was 50 percent above TNT's closing price on the previous day, and described as generous by most analysts.
A number of other funds have recently reduced their TNT holdings, including JP Morgan Investment Management.
The KPN bid for TNT is conditional on the Dutch company receiving at least 90 percent of the ordinary shares of TNT.
